increased ERK responses in RA T cells facilitate responses to suboptimum stimulation and that treatment with a MEK- 1/2 inhibitor delays arthritis onset and reduces disease severity.

the ERK pathway is hyperactivated in RA T cells, and this is a general feature of RA that is not related to disease activity, and that this hyperactivation is sufficient to induce autoimmunity in a mouse model and can be therapeutically targeted to prevent disease.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which the T cell receptor (TCR) senses and transduces signals from the environment to the T cell.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the activation threshold of the TCR.
the molecular mechanisms of T cell receptor signaling and the role of these pathways in the pathogenesis and prevention of autoimmunity in humans and animal models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ERK phosphorylation is a key factor for the development of autoimmune diseases.
the increased TCR signaling observed in RA patients, which is also observed in the SKG animal model, may be a contributing factor to the disease and may be a therapeutic target.
TCR threshold calibration in RA is a consequence of increased ERK signaling, which delays the recruitment of the TCR phosphatase SHP-1 and facilitates responses to suboptimum stimulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
T cells in patients with RA have a defect in their ability to calibrate TCR thresholds.
we show a defect in T cell tolerance in RA that is mediated by an increased ERK phosphorylating threshold.
T cells in RA patients and SKG mice have an increased TCR signaling threshold due to increased TCR-induced ERK activity that results in increased TCR-induced Zap-70 and NF- κB signaling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
increased ERK activation contributes to T cell tolerance breakdown and disease in RA and that targeting the ERK pathway could be a novel treatment for RA and other T cell-mediated diseases.
increased responsiveness of the TCR-ERK pathway in T cells from patients with rheumatoid arthritis is a disease-associated trait.
increased ERK activity is an important factor in the pathogenesis of autoimmune disease.
